newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Zaire refugee exodus sends signal to Tanzania.
newsitem.headline: Zaire refugee exodus sends signal to Tanzania.

text.p: The mass return of Rwandan Hutu refugees from Zaire could encourage 540,000 kinfolk in Tanzania camps to go home as well, the U.N. refugee agency said.

"I think it ought to be an encouraging signal, but whether it will or not remains to be seen. I'm very optimistic it will send the right message," Vincent Parker, Tanzania spokesman for UNHCR, said on Friday.

"I think they (Rwandan refugees in Tanzania) will wait until the 400,000 have marched into Rwanda, moved into their respective communes and heard correspondence that all is well," Parker told Reuters.
Latest UNHCR statistics put at 539,986 the number of Rwandan Hutu refugees in Tanzania in addition to 122,158 Burundian Hutu refugees.

Like the 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees in Zaire before Friday's exodus home, those in Tanzania fled their homeland in 1994 to escape advancing Tutsi rebels who are now in government in Kigali. Many of the refugees also feared reprisals for their part in the 1994 genocide of Rwandan Tutsis.
The total of refugees in Tanzania increased slightly this month because of an influx across Lake Tanganyika due to fighting in eastern Zaire between Zairean rebels and the army, Parker said.
So far this month 26,839 refugees, almost all Zairean nationals, have been registered in west Tanzania's Kigoma district.
Before last month's rebellion 730,000 Rwandan refugees lived in Zaire's North Kivu province, while 300,000 were housed around Bukavu in South Kivu, UNHCR says.
A total of 200,000 lived in camps north of South Kivu's Uvira of which 144,000 were Burundian Hutus who fled Burundi's civil war. Since the rebellion 40,000 Burundian Hutus have gone home.
Parker cautioned the circumstances which sparked the exodus from North Kivu's Mugunga camp did not apply to Rwandans living in camps in Tanzania where there is no fighting and aid is not in jeopardy.
He added: "We should not lose sight that we've got intimidators in a number of camps in Tanzania. The grip of intimidators is still quite firm."
Hutu extremists, including the Interahamwe militia behind the Rwandan genocide of 1994, opposed the repatriation of refugees fearing it could erode their support base.
A lightning advance by Zairean rebels who now control a 300-kilometre (180 mile) strip of territory in east Zaire prompted the return of Rwandan Hutu refugees.
Hutu extremists lost their grip on the mass of refugees after being dislodged from the camps.
Tanzania has expressed irritation at the presence of Rwandan refugees on its soil, but has taken no steps to expel Rwandan or Burundian refugees.
